title: Pit Crews, Seven C’s, and AI: Mirat Dave and Danish Butt from Swiftwater & Co.
author: Mirat Dave · Danish Butt

st.t: Legal leadership: Business capability complements legal expertise
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s operational-leadership proposition by recommending a specific approach to global process standardisation: preserve a common workflow while accommodating genuine jurisdictional differences. Its resistance anecdote also identifies an implementation barrier, while remaining only a single experience rather than evidence of universal lawyer resistance.
qs: And so let’s focus on how we integrate those differences into a standard process.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The commentary aligns with the cluster’s move beyond raw efficiency or model capability by emphasizing workflow-specific value, output quality and better data. It materially extends that proposition into pricing, suggesting that individual legal workflows may increasingly be priced according to their value and efficiency gains, although it offers forecasts rather than evidence of reliable delivery or realised outcomes.
qs: both at law firms where there’s the potential for pricing changes, a lot of momentum towards looking at the value of legal work, not by the billable hour, although the billable hour will still be essential for calculating alternative fee arrangements, but more about how do you really look at individual workflows and what makes sense from a pricing perspective for those workflows.
So actually greater value from your lawyers, from the client perspective, higher quality output, access to better data, and so on.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Swiftwater accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI value depends on selective deployment and operating-model redesign, then extends it with a concrete investigation-operations approach: standardise common processes, prepare data, define business-aligned outcomes and adopt a coordinated long-term strategy before scaling tools. Its capacity and quality claims are largely predictions rather than demonstrated results, and it gives limited attention to verification.
qs: And that’s where things like standardizing processes, and I alluded to that a little bit across the world, instead of having different approaches to investigations for EMEA or for Italy specifically or for Singapore or for Hong Kong, et cetera, how can I align because I recognize 80, 90 % of it is the same and there’s only nuances?
And on the other end it’s like, okay, let’s try every tool under the sun and you get mediocre results because there’s no strategy.

kp.k: Legal AI funding and platform shifts remain speculative
kp.d: In her ILTACon overview, Nikki Shaver reports a banker's expectation of continuing legal-technology investment because the total addressable market exceeds outside funders' expectations. She also describes speculation that new AI-centered work platforms could displace Outlook and document management systems as lawyers' primary working environments, with newer vendors potentially replacing established suppliers. These are conference observations and forecasts, not demonstrated market outcomes.
qs: A bit of insight from one of the bankers is this bubble is not going to burst anytime soon.
So we should expect to see continuing funding rounds in the legal for the next few years at least.
the players we’ve really seen as mature and enduring may not necessarily be the core vendors in the industry anymore

kp.k: Firms experiment with AI teams and workflow pricing
kp.d: Shaver reports firms upskilling employees and hiring AI specialists into IT, innovation, or independent firm-wide departments. She observes momentum toward workflow-specific pricing that reflects efficiency gains and legal-work value, while retaining billable-hour calculations for alternative fee arrangements. She also describes a shift in expected AI returns from efficiency alone toward higher-quality output and better data access for clients.
qs: A lot of firms grappling with how to handle AI and actually upskilling internally, but also hiring people specifically.
sometimes sitting within IT, sometimes within innovation, and sometimes creating an entirely new department, spanning the entire firm, sitting independently.
although the billable hour will still be essential for calculating alternative fee arrangements
higher quality output, access to better data, and so on.

kp.k: Standardization and AI could expand capacity without hiring
kp.d: Mirat Dave contrasts linear investigation capacity from adding staff with what he calls exponential capacity from combining standardized processes, technology, and AI. He argues that cross-border differences can often be integrated into common processes: he initially estimates 60, 70, 80 % commonality and later describes 80, 90 % commonality for investigations. His claims of greater capacity, quality, consistency, speed, and reduced risk are practitioner assertions without measured implementation results in the transcript.
qs: often 60, 70, 80 % of things can be done exactly the same.
how can I align because I recognize 80, 90 % of it is the same and there’s only nuances?
when you start combining those, you start gaining exponential capacity.
And so you’re able to handle that growth without increasing headcount.

kp.k: Transformation budgets require understandable investment cases
kp.d: Dave reports resistance to process and technology change because additional headcount is a familiar, understandable expense, whereas systems implementation and consulting are harder to justify. He recommends structured explanations of cost, savings, capacity, and ROI for budget owners. He says clients receiving help with these cases are often more successful, but later qualifies that even a strong case must compete with other investments.
qs: I can’t get budget for an IT project. I can’t get budget for consulting, but I can somehow get budget for more people.
how much it’s actually gonna cost, how much it’s actually going to save, what’s the ROI.
Doesn’t mean you’re guaranteed to get that money because you know, there’s 50 things on the plate and there’s only X amount of money

kp.k: Business-value metrics lag behind activity measures
kp.d: Danish Butt recounts an unspecified benchmarking discussion in which 90 % measured investigation numbers, 80 % measured duration, and only 5%, 10% reported measures such as revenue or reputation saved; no sample size, methodology, or date is supplied. He argues that valuable outcomes are harder to measure because systems and information are disconnected. His IP example contrasts counting patents and renewals with identifying the most profitable patent, which requires product-level connections.

kp.k: Legal operations should prioritize value and stakeholder trust
kp.d: Butt recommends judging legal, risk, and compliance operations by stakeholder value rather than cost savings, technology implementation, or recognition alone. He warns that imposing technology on the strength of benchmarks can erode trust if it does not improve users' work, and that efficiency mandates can overlook staff stress and downstream effects. He presents this as a service-oriented operating philosophy, not a measured AI outcome.
qs: Focus on value and focus on, you know, just not doing it faster, better, cheaper.
You’re going to use it because benchmarks say so.
you didn’t improve my life. You may have great benchmarks.
it doesn’t take into account your people who may be under stress

kp.k: Pit-crew analogy reframes legal functions as business enablers
kp.d: Dave argues that legal, compliance, risk, and investigation functions should move beyond enforcement and procedural checking to proactively improving the business. His F1 pit-crew analogy emphasizes behind-the-scenes contributions to frontline success through speed, agility, and responsiveness. He distinguishes second-line functions from internal audit and recommends aligning investment requests and performance measures with C-suite priorities such as growth, margin, assets, and purpose. He acknowledges that traditional structures and incentives often discourage this approach.
qs: You’re a line two function. You’re not an auditor. That’s why you have internal audit.
think of your function as a pit crew in an F1 race.
The driver’s not getting there without the pit crew.
And oftentimes the incentives aren’t there.
The functional leaders need to start speaking the language of the C-suite.

kp.k: Contract-renewal example illustrates proactive legal business support
kp.d: Dave describes an unnamed large government contractor for which 20 % of growth and new revenue came from existing contracts. Legal, risk, and compliance initially focused on renewal procedures rather than renewal success. Following CFO-sponsored intervention, the teams used their business-wide visibility to distribute best practices and prompt relationship-building and value communication six and four months before renewal. Dave reports a substantial increase in renewal success but provides no quantified improvement or AI attribution.
qs: 20 % of their growth and new revenue came from existing contracts
they weren’t invested in the success or failure of those renewals.
You’ve got this contract coming up in six months, you need to start thinking about this. Four months out, you need to start thinking about this.
they saw a tremendous increase in the percentage of contract renewals and the success rate.

kp.k: Investigation analytics could prevent recurring problems
kp.d: Drawing on current work with a couple of clients, Dave recommends analyzing allegations by personnel level, business unit, geography, regulation, and timing rather than merely processing individual cases. He argues that correlations can identify business changes that should reduce risk, incoming allegations, and investigation workload. This is a proposed mechanism and expected benefit, not a quantified finding or a specifically demonstrated AI deployment.
qs: we’re working with a couple of clients right now
What business units are they coming from? What geographies are they coming from? Are they related to specific regulations?
And then you start doing correlations and you’re able to actually go back to the business and say, hey, you here’s what you need to improve.
So you’re reducing your workload, but you’re effectively making the business operate with less risk.

kp.k: AI adoption needs strategy alongside targeted use cases
kp.d: Butt predicts many pointed AI use cases rather than one overarching solution over the next four or five years, with different tools suited to different problems. He nevertheless urges organizations to treat AI as a sustained professional way of working, supported by a two-year strategy, enterprise data integration, data preparation, and knowledgeable hires. He cautions against both blanket prohibitions and indiscriminate tool experimentation that produces mediocre results without strategy.

kp.k: AI may turn investigation repositories into working platforms
kp.d: In the one-to-two-year outlook discussion, Dave predicts AI-assisted allegation triage, investigation-plan drafting, and interview-question tailoring by misconduct type. He estimates that reading an allegation and identifying participants could produce 70, 80 % of a plan, but supplies no test evidence and notes that some functionality does not require AI. He expects investigation platforms to evolve from recording completed work toward facilitating it over the next two years, while questioning whether vague adoption mandates will deliver meaningful change.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nikki Shaver anticipates continued legal-AI investment and reports firms building dedicated AI capabilities.
pts.d: In her opening ILTACon overview (00:00–03:29), Shaver predicts continuing legal-sector funding rounds for at least several years, linking this to a larger-than-anticipated total addressable market. She also reports current internal upskilling and AI-specific hiring, with teams located in IT, innovation, or independent firm-wide departments. Her funding outlook draws partly on an unnamed banker's assessment; it is not presented as an independently documented investment forecast.

pts.k: Shaver predicts that new AI-era work platforms may displace established core systems and incumbent vendors.
pts.d: Shaver describes a possible shift from Outlook and document-management systems as lawyers' principal working environments toward platforms into which existing repositories feed data. She further suggests that recent entrants could become enduring core vendors at the expense of established suppliers. These are explicitly possibilities and conference-derived expectations, not reports of completed displacement.

pts.k: Shaver reports movement toward workflow-specific, value-oriented pricing and a broader conception of AI returns than efficiency alone.
pts.d: In the opening overview, Shaver connects potential pricing changes to workflow-level efficiency gains. She does not predict complete abandonment of time-based calculations: she explicitly retains a role for the billable hour in calculating alternative fee arrangements. She also reports a shift in how AI's value is understood, toward higher-quality lawyer output and better access to data for clients. No measured ROI or pricing-change figures are supplied.

pts.k: Mirat Dave claims that combining process standardization, technology, and AI can expand investigation capacity without proportionate headcount growth.
pts.d: At 09:52–12:52, Dave contrasts linear staffing expansion with what he calls 'exponential capacity' from standardized processes combined with technology and AI. He anticipates better quality, consistency, speed, and reduced risk as well as capacity gains. The claim is conditional on process redesign and integration, rather than AI adoption alone. He offers a consulting-based operational argument, not a measured capacity curve or documented AI deployment result; his quality claim is qualified as probable.

pts.k: Danish Butt expects AI adoption to involve many narrowly targeted use cases rather than a single overarching solution.
pts.d: At approximately 19:26–20:59, Butt predicts multiple pointed use cases for different problems over at least the next four or five years. Different solutions will work best for different tasks, creating a continuing need for advisors to track which approaches work and how they improve. He embeds this prediction in an argument that legal, risk, and compliance functions should prioritize business value over merely doing work faster or more cheaply.

pts.k: Butt predicts a shift from AI as an isolated tool to AI as an integrated professional way of working, contingent on enterprise strategy and preparation.
pts.d: At 37:29–40:10, Butt argues that AI should become part of a broader operating approach rather than simply replace search or research tools. He sees an opportunity to integrate legal functions more closely with enterprise data, informing claims and investigations in ways previously unavailable. He warns that indiscriminate experimentation produces mediocre results without strategy, while a tools-only approach risks an incoherent collection of technology three years later. He recommends a two-year roadmap, data preparation, and knowledgeable hires. The transcript's hope that hallucinations will disappear is presented as an attitude among tool users, not an unqualified Butt prediction.

pts.k: Dave predicts AI-assisted investigation planning and tailored interview preparation, alongside platforms that actively support work rather than merely record it.
pts.d: At 40:29–43:44, Dave proposes using allegation type and the people involved to generate an initial investigation plan, estimating that 70–80% of the plan could be completed this way. He also describes tailoring interview questions to categories such as bribery, harassment, and financial misconduct. He expects these capabilities to reduce preparation work and improve consistency, speed, and capacity, becoming embedded in investigation platforms over the next two years. His framing is assistance and partial preparation, not demonstrated autonomous investigation. He expressly doubts how far actual adoption will progress and notes that some functionality does not require AI, although AI makes it easier. At 43:44, Butt says Swiftwater is building a next-generation investigation-centric tool; this is a development statement, not evidence that the projected capabilities have been delivered.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The AI claims rest chiefly on conference observations, consulting experience, illustrative workflows, and predictions rather than documented performance studies.
pts.d: Claims 1–3 draw on Shaver's ILTACon observations, industry conversations, and an unnamed banker's view. Claims 4–7 draw on Dave's and Butt's advisory experience and conceptual examples. Dave's conversation with an attorney at a large bank illustrates unclear adoption direction; it does not measure AI effectiveness. The 70–80% planning estimate is unsupported by a cited trial, and 'exponential capacity' is not quantified. Elsewhere, Butt cites unspecified investigation-measurement benchmarks, and Dave recounts improved contract renewals following operational redesign, but neither establishes an AI-caused outcome. Dave also reports personally using AI summaries to keep up with information before reading interesting original sources. Swiftwater's stated tool-development work supplies commercial context for the platform forecast, not independent validation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source distinguishes current adoption trends from several overlapping forward-looking horizons and repeatedly conditions benefits on organizational readiness.
pts.d: Relative to the document's supplied 2025 date, Shaver describes current team-building and expects funding for at least the next few years; her platform and pricing scenarios have no firm deadline. Dave's capacity argument has no specified realization date and depends on standardization plus technology and AI. Butt expects targeted use cases for at least four or five years, recommends a two-year strategy, and warns of tool fragmentation three years out. Dave explicitly forecasts investigation functionality and platform transformation over two years while expressing uncertainty about uptake. Budget approval, demonstrable business value, data readiness, knowledgeable personnel, and coherent strategy are recurring conditions. Dave notes that better investment framing increases the likelihood of funding but does not guarantee it.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law firms and their clients, legal-technology vendors and investors, and corporate legal, risk, compliance, and investigation teams.
pts.d: For firms, Shaver anticipates AI-specific hiring, upskilling, changing working environments, and possible workflow-based pricing changes; clients may receive higher-quality and more data-informed work. Vendors face possible changes in market leadership, while investors are presented with continuing funding opportunities. On the buyer side, Dave and Butt focus on general counsel, legal operations, investigators, risk and compliance leaders, and corporate budget owners. These groups may gain capacity without additional headcount, reduce preparation work, and connect legal activity more closely to enterprise outcomes. Advisors face continuing learning demands. The headcount claim concerns avoiding additional hiring as workload grows, not a specific prediction of layoffs. The discussion does not establish effects on access to justice, consumer legal services, or law-firm staffing hierarchies.
